faq.a: They bridge the gap between scarce facilities and patients, delivering meds, monitoring side effects and reducing travel burden.
faq.q: Why are community health workers essential for psychiatric care?

faq.a: Identify an equivalent on the essential medicines list and obtain it from the nearest district pharmacy or partner NGO.
faq.q: What is the first step when a required antipsychotic is out of stock?

faq.a: Keep a log of missed doses, referral delays and stock‑out dates; present aggregated data to district health managers.

exam: What immediate action should you take for a psychotic patient when haloperidol is unavailable? — Obtain the nearest WHO‑listed alternative (e.g., chlorpromazine) or arrange urgent referral to a stocked facility.
How does a weak referral network contribute to repeated emergency presentations? — Delays prevent continuity of care, leading to relapse and crisis visits.
Explain why task‑sharing with nurses improves mental health outcomes in low‑resource settings. — It expands prescribing capacity, reduces travel time and maintains treatment continuity.
A patient reports missing doses for two weeks; what system factor should you explore first? — Check the pharmacy stock‑log for recent antipsychotic shortages.
Distinguish between patient non‑adherence and medication stock‑out as causes of relapse. — Non‑adherence is intentional; stock‑out is external and documented by pharmacy records.
What red‑flag signs demand urgent transfer to a tertiary psychiatric unit? — Acute suicidality, uncontrolled aggression, or severe psychosis with no safe community options.
How would you use a CHW to prevent relapse after discharge in a rural setting? — Arrange weekly home visits for pill counts, side‑effect checks and crisis planning.
Why is it important to report system failures even if the patient is currently stable? — Early reporting triggers resupply, prevents future crises and supports health‑system planning.
ai.title: Health Systems in Psychiatry
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Health systems shape access to mental health care, especially in low‑resource East African settings. Understanding system gaps, referral pathways and resource‑limited interventions helps clinicians provide realistic, patient‑centred care.

b: Components: governance, financing, workforce, medicines, information, service delivery
Key indicator: proportion of people with severe mental illness receiving continuous care
sections.p: Health systems refer to the organized network of institutions, workforce, financing and policies that deliver mental health services. In psychiatry, diagnosis of system failure is clinical – patients repeatedly miss appointments, medications are unavailable, or referrals break down.

b: Stage 1: intermittent medication gaps
Stage 2: chronic referral delays (>4 weeks)
Stage 3: complete lack of mental health services
sections.p: Systemic barriers can be staged from mild (occasional stock‑outs) to severe (no mental health provider within 100 km). Staging guides escalation: community health worker (CHW) support → district referral → tertiary psychiatric unit.

b: Limited financing – mental health budgets <1 % of health budget
Workforce shortage – <0.1 psychiatrist per 100 000 population
Supply‑chain failures – essential psychotropics out of stock
Stigma and low community awareness
Weak referral networks and transport barriers
sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa the most common drivers of a broken psychiatric health system are:

b: Repeated emergency presentations for agitation
Medication gaps reported by caregivers
Long travel distances to the nearest mental health clinic

sections.p: When system failures are severe, patients risk rapid deterioration, self‑harm, or violent behaviour.

sections.p: Management is dual: treat the patient and strengthen the system.

Create a local crisis plan with family and community leaders

sections.p: A normal mental‑status exam does not rule out imminent system failure.

Severe agitation requiring restraint when no medication is available
